templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Plains spadefoot toads and Mexican spadefoot toads breed in the same temporary ponds in the southwestern United States, and the two species sometimes interbreed, although hybrids come at a cost: hybrid males are often sterile, and hybrid females lay fewer eggs. Hybrid tadpoles, however, develop faster than plains spadefoot tadpoles do, though more slowly than Mexican spadefoot tadpoles. In experiments by biologist Karin Pfennig, plains spadefoot females in deep water usually favored the calls of males of their own species, whereas females in shallow water, which dries up sooner, displayed no such preference.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about plains spadefoot females in shallow water?
options: They likely respond to Mexican spadefoot males’ calls because those calls carry farther over shallow water than over deep water.
They likely choose Mexican spadefoot males over males of their own species because hybrid tadpoles develop as quickly as Mexican spadefoot tadpoles do.
They likely accept males of either species because, where a pond may soon dry up, faster development can outweigh the drawbacks of hybrid young.
They likely produce fewer hybrid offspring than females in deep water do, since hybrid tadpoles develop too slowly to survive in drying ponds.
items.explanation: The text says hybrids are less fertile but that hybrid tadpoles develop faster than plains spadefoot tadpoles, and that females in shallow water, which dries up sooner, showed no preference for males of their own species. Together these suggest that where a pond may dry before tadpoles mature, the hybrids’ faster development can make up for their reduced fertility, so these females accept either kind of male.

A.why_wrong: The text ties shallow water to drying up sooner, not to how calls travel; nothing is said about sound carrying.

B.why_wrong: Females in shallow water showed no preference rather than a preference for Mexican males, and the text says hybrid tadpoles develop more slowly than Mexican spadefoot tadpoles.

D.why_wrong: Hybrid tadpoles develop faster than plains tadpoles, and shallow-water females lack the own-species preference that limits hybrid matings in deep water, so they would likely produce more hybrids, not fewer.

sources.what: Pfennig 2007 (Science): plains spadefoot females favored own species about 65% of the time in deep water and showed no preference in shallow pools; Mexican tadpoles develop faster, hybrids in between; hybrid males often sterile, hybrid females lay fewer eggs

items.notes: Natural science (behavioral ecology). P1 hybrids less fertile but develop faster than plains tadpoles; P2 shallow water dries sooner and there females lose their own-species preference; unstated conclusion: a trade-off favoring speed where ponds dry fast. Source says hybrids are intermediate, so the passage keeps them slower than Mexican tadpoles; it says no preference, not a preference for Mexican males. Karin Pfennig also appears (with others) in inferences.S7.medium.w2b2_18 on a different subject (kingsnake mimicry).

band7.why: Planned band 6. Two links (shallow ponds dry sooner; hybrid tadpoles develop faster than plains tadpoles) to an unstated trade-off; key paraphrased (faster development can outweigh the drawbacks). A keeps a foothold (they do respond to Mexican calls) with an invented mechanism, B and D reverse the development comparison; each wrong option still falls to one stated fact. Options 22 to 25 words, no stance word: band 6, not stronger.

items.passage: Most pitcher plants in Borneo obtain much of their nitrogen by trapping insects in pitchers filled with digestive fluid, but the pitchers of Nepenthes hemsleyana are long, hold relatively little fluid, and capture far fewer insects than those of related species. Ecologist T. Ulmar Grafe and colleagues found that Hardwicke’s woolly bats roost in these pitchers during the day, resting above the fluid, into which their droppings fall. By comparing plants that hosted bats with plants that did not, the team determined that the hosts obtained a substantial share of their nitrogen from those droppings.
items.stem: Based on the text, what is most likely true about Nepenthes hemsleyana?
options: Its bat tenants likely make up for a nutrient shortfall that results from its pitchers’ weakness as traps.
Its pitchers likely hold little fluid because a deeper pool would break down the bats’ droppings before the plant could absorb them.
It likely catches more insects in pitchers where bats roost, since the bats’ presence draws insects into those pitchers.
It likely gets more nitrogen from bat droppings than any related pitcher plant gets from the insects it traps.
items.explanation: The text says pitcher plants usually obtain nitrogen from insects they trap, that this plant’s pitchers catch far fewer insects than related plants’ pitchers, and that plants hosting bats get a substantial share of their nitrogen from bat droppings. Together these suggest that the bats help make up for the nitrogen the plant’s pitchers fail to obtain from insects.

B.why_wrong: The pitchers do hold little fluid, but the text gives no reason for this and says nothing about fluid breaking down droppings.

C.why_wrong: Bats do roost in the pitchers, but the text never says they draw insects in; it says the pitchers catch far fewer insects than related plants’ pitchers.

D.why_wrong: The text says bats supply a substantial share of this plant’s nitrogen; it never compares that amount with what other pitcher plants get from insects.

sources.what: Grafe et al. 2011 (Biology Letters), National Geographic report: the long-pitchered Nepenthes (now N. hemsleyana) is at least seven times less effective at catching insects, has less digestive fluid, hosts roosting Hardwicke’s woolly bats, and gets about a third of its nitrogen from their droppings; the 2011 report calls the plant N. rafflesiana elongata (since described as N. hemsleyana); nitrogen share found by comparing occupied plants with unoccupied controls (at least 34 percent)

items.notes: Natural science (mutualism). P1 pitcher plants usually get nitrogen from insects; P2 this one catches far fewer insects; P3 bat droppings supply much of its nitrogen; conclusion: the bats compensate. Different subject from the official Nepenthes pudica item (underground pitchers, another skill); the bat mutualism is not used anywhere in the bank (grep Hardwicke, hemsleyana).

fixes: method sentence: the passage said the droppings falling into the pitchers let the team determine the nitrogen share; the source says they compared plants with bats against unoccupied controls; now the comparison is the method and the falling droppings the mechanism
sources note: the 2011 report names the plant N. rafflesiana elongata (since described as N. hemsleyana); at least 34 percent of nitrogen confirmed

band7.why: Planned band 6. Three statements joined (usual nitrogen source, weak traps, nitrogen from droppings) into an unstated compensation; key abstracted (nutrient shortfall, weakness as traps). B and D keep a true foothold (little fluid; nitrogen from droppings) and fail on an invented cause or comparison, C is unsupported. No stance word: strong band 6.

items.passage: Much of what archaeologists know about early humans comes from stone tools, partly because stone endures across vast spans of time, whereas wood usually decays. At Kalambo Falls in Zambia, however, a team that included archaeologist Larry Barham recovered two logs that had been deliberately worked so that they fit together, forming part of a structure, possibly a platform near the water. The wood was dated to at least 476,000 years ago, before the earliest known evidence of our own species, Homo sapiens.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about early humans’ use of wood?
options: It was likely more extensive than their use of stone, which would explain why relatively few of their stone tools have been found.
It likely began before they learned to shape stone into tools, as the age of the Kalambo Falls logs indicates.
It was likely devoted mainly to building platforms near water, given the setting of the Kalambo Falls logs.
It was likely more advanced than a record made up mostly of stone tools would suggest.
items.explanation: The text says that knowledge of early humans comes largely from stone tools because wood usually decays, and that a rare surviving find shows people deliberately shaping logs into a structure 476,000 years ago. Together these suggest that their woodworking was more advanced than a record built mostly from stone tools would indicate.

A.why_wrong: The text says much of what is known comes from stone tools, so their stone tools have not been scarce; it also never compares how extensively they used wood and stone.

B.why_wrong: The logs predate Homo sapiens, but the text says nothing about when early humans began making stone tools, so it gives no basis for this order.

C.why_wrong: The text describes one structure that was possibly a platform near water; it gives no basis for saying what their woodworking was mainly used for.

sources.what: Kalambo Falls (Zambia): two worked wooden beams forming an interlocking structure, possibly a platform by a water source, at least 476,000 years old, predating Homo sapiens; Larry Barham among the discoverers; wood decays quickly so little survives (Barham et al. 2023, Nature)

items.notes: Archaeology. P1 the record leans on stone because wood decays; P2 a rare wooden survival shows deliberate joinery 476,000 years ago; conclusion: woodworking skill is underrepresented. No notch named (the Wikipedia source says worked, interlocking beams). Paper: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06557-9.

band7.why: Planned band 6. Two links (the record leans on stone because wood decays; deliberate joinery 476,000 years ago) to an unstated underrepresentation; key is the shortest option and abstracts the record. A dies on one stated fact (much is known from stone tools), B on missing stone-tool dates, C generalizes one find. Band 6.

review.note: topic fame borderline: the 2023 Kalambo Falls find had front-page coverage (oldest wooden structure) and sits just past the official 2022 date range; kept, since the item turns on the stone-record inference, not the headline

items.passage: Discussions of how false beliefs spread online often treat two situations as if they were one. In what philosopher C. Thi Nguyen calls an epistemic bubble, relevant voices have simply been left out, perhaps by chance, so members never encounter certain information and arguments; in an echo chamber, by contrast, outside voices have been deliberately discredited, and members have learned to distrust every source beyond the group. The distinction matters, Nguyen argues, because the two call for different remedies: giving people access to evidence they have missed can dissolve a bubble, but it may only strengthen an echo chamber.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Nguyen argues that epistemic bubbles are harder to escape than echo chambers, since members of bubbles do not realize that any voices have been left out.
Nguyen contends that bubbles and echo chambers need different treatment, since evidence that can break up a bubble may backfire in an echo chamber, whose members distrust outsiders.
According to Nguyen, an epistemic bubble turns into an echo chamber once its members have gone long enough without hearing other views.
Nguyen claims that, because both structures keep members from hearing outside voices, giving people access to a wider range of evidence is the most reliable way to correct either one.
items.explanation: The text distinguishes bubbles, where voices are merely left out, from echo chambers, whose members have learned to distrust every outside source, and says the distinction matters because the two call for different remedies: evidence that can dissolve a bubble may only strengthen an echo chamber. Choice B joins the distinction, the different remedies, and the reason for them, and keeps the text’s hedge.

A.why_wrong: The text says exposure can break up a bubble but may strengthen an echo chamber, which makes echo chambers the harder ones to escape.

C.why_wrong: The text treats the two as distinct structures and never says one turns into the other.

D.recipe: overstated, contradicts for one case (half-true premise)
D.why_wrong: The text says access to evidence may only strengthen an echo chamber, so it is not a reliable remedy for both; and echo chambers work by teaching members to distrust outside voices, not merely by keeping those voices out.

sources.what: Nguyen, Echo Chambers and Epistemic Bubbles (Episteme 2020): bubbles leave voices out, echo chambers actively discredit them and bring members to distrust outside sources; mere exposure to evidence can shatter a bubble but may reinforce an echo chamber

items.notes: Social science / philosophy (social epistemology). Scholar-argument passage, spread structure: definitions in sentences 2 and 3, the governing claim in 4. Key keeps the hedge (may). A different Nguyen work (Games: Agency as Art) is claimed by central_ideas_and_details.T1.hard.w3b2_04; this is a different subject.

fixes: key carried only the echo-chamber consequence, reachable from the last sentence alone; now joins the distinction, the different remedies and the distrust reason, paraphrased (break up, backfire), hedge kept
D given a half-true premise (both structures keep outside voices away) so it is not killed by the last sentence alone; explanation and D why_wrong aligned; re-solved blind, B only

band7.why: Planned band 6. After the fix the key joins three statements (bubble definition, echo-chamber distrust, different remedies) and is paraphrased; A is a reversal with a plausible reason, C an invented process, D a half-true premise with a contradicted conclusion. Options 23 to 30 words against a band-7 main-idea median of 34, no stance word: strong band 6.

items.passage: Footbinding in China has often been explained in terms of beauty and marriage: bound feet, the conventional account holds, signaled refinement and improved a girl’s prospects. Anthropologists Laurel Bossen and Hill Gates, drawing on interviews with thousands of elderly women in rural China, argue that this account overlooks the practice’s economic role. In their view, binding kept girls seated indoors, where mothers could train them in spinning, weaving, and other handwork for the household, so when machine-made textiles diminished the value of such handwork in the early twentieth century, one important reason for footbinding disappeared.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Bossen and Gates suggest that footbinding in rural China owed much to the economic value of girls’ handwork, not only to ideals of beauty.
Bossen and Gates show that footbinding was more common in rural China than in cities, where machine-made textiles became available earlier.
Although footbinding improved girls’ marriage prospects, Bossen and Gates found that it ended mainly because handwork came to be valued more highly.
Bossen and Gates argue that footbinding declined once rural families recognized that the practice kept girls from contributing to household income.
items.explanation: The text sets the usual explanation (beauty and marriage) against Bossen and Gates’s argument that binding kept girls at household handwork and lost one of its reasons when machine-made textiles reduced the value of that work. Choice A states this revision while keeping the older explanation in view.

B.why_wrong: The text mentions machine-made textiles but never compares how common footbinding was in rural areas and cities.

C.why_wrong: The text says machine-made textiles reduced the value of handwork; it does not say handwork came to be valued more highly.

D.why_wrong: In Bossen and Gates’s view binding kept girls at handwork for the household, so it did not keep them from contributing; the practice lost a reason when that handwork lost value.

sources.what: Bossen and Gates, Bound Feet, Young Hands (2017): interviews with thousands of elderly rural women; bound girls kept indoors at spinning and weaving; footbinding a means to reserve women to handwork; mechanized textile production removed a reason to maintain it

items.notes: History / social science (anthropology). View then correction; key carries both halves (economic role, not only beauty). Wikipedia also notes John Shepherd’s challenge to the handicraft thesis, so the passage keeps everything attributed (argue, in their view).

band7.why: Planned band 6. View then correction; key carries both halves (economic value of handwork, not only beauty) in its own words. B invents a rural and urban comparison, C and D reverse the handwork logic while keeping true details (textiles, household handwork). No stance word: band 6.

items.passage: In the 1850s, as New York City acquired land for Central Park, newspapers described the residents of Seneca Village, a settlement inside the park’s planned boundaries, as squatters living in shanties, but records and excavations tell a different story. Founded in 1825 when free African Americans began purchasing lots there, the village had several churches and a school, and by 1850 more than half of its Black residents owned property. Excavations by a team led by archaeologists Diana Wall and Nan Rothschild have uncovered house foundations along with everyday household objects.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Seneca Village was founded in 1825, when free African Americans began buying lots on land that later fell within Central Park’s boundaries.
Newspapers of the 1850s described Seneca Village’s homes accurately but overlooked how many of its residents owned property.
Seneca Village was a stable community in which many residents owned land, not the makeshift settlement that newspapers of the 1850s portrayed.
Seneca Village’s churches and school drew free African Americans from across New York City, which is why so many residents owned property there.
items.explanation: The text opens with how newspapers of the 1850s portrayed Seneca Village (squatters in shanties) and then says records and excavations tell a different story: residents bought lots, built churches and a school, and often owned property, and excavations found house foundations. Choice C states the correction and the portrayal it corrects: a settled community of many landowners, not a makeshift settlement.

A.why_wrong: The village was founded this way, but this is one detail; the text’s point is that the village was a settled, property-owning community despite how newspapers portrayed it.

B.why_wrong: Many residents did own property, but the text says records and excavations tell a different story from the newspapers’ account, and the excavations found house foundations, so it does not present the newspapers’ description of the homes as accurate.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions the churches and the school as signs of an established community; it never says they drew people from across the city or explains property ownership by them.

sources.what: Seneca Village: founded 1825 by free Black Americans buying land; churches and schools; more than half of Black residents owned property by 1850; press and park advocates called residents squatters and the area shantytowns; razed 1857 for Central Park; excavations by Diana Wall, Nan Rothschild and team found foundations and household objects

items.notes: History (with archaeology). View then correction; the item does not hinge on the ownership figure (more than half of Black residents by 1850, from the source).

fixes: key echoed the passage (squatters, owned property); now paraphrased (a stable community of many landowners, not a makeshift settlement)

A (invented comparison) and D (life after clearing) each died on missing support; A is now a true but narrow detail (the 1825 founding), D an invented cause built from true details (churches, school, property); B reworded as half-true; explanation aligned; re-solved blind, C only
review.note: topic fame borderline: Seneca Village has had mainstream coverage since the 2019 Central Park exhibit, but it is not textbook or viral; kept

band7.why: Planned band 6. After the fix the key is paraphrased and two distractors are true details (A) or built from them (D), so the reader must choose scope rather than spot a false fact; B is half-true. Options 18 to 23 words: band 6.

items.passage: The Rule of Saint Benedict, which governed communal life in many medieval monasteries, restricted when and where monks were permitted to speak, and throughout the night an especially strict silence was observed. To communicate during such periods, monks relied on hand signs, and inventories of these signs survive from the Abbey of Cluny in France, the earliest compiled around 1075. Historians observe that the signs were predominantly nouns designating things in the monks’ daily existence, such as foods, garments, rooms, and liturgical objects; signs for actions, such as “sit,” “kneel,” and “confess,” were comparatively scarce.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about the signs recorded in the lists from Cluny?
options: They allowed monks to carry on long conversations during the nighttime silence.
Most of them referred to objects and places that were part of monastic life.
They were invented at Cluny and later adopted by monasteries elsewhere.
They included more signs for actions than for the things monks used.
items.explanation: The text says the signs were mostly nouns for things in the monks’ daily lives, such as foods, garments, rooms, and liturgical objects. Choice B restates this.

A.why_wrong: The signs were mostly nouns with few signs for actions, and the text never says they were used for long conversations.

C.why_wrong: The text says the earliest surviving lists come from Cluny, not that the signs were invented there or spread from there.

D.why_wrong: The text says signs for actions were comparatively few and most signs were nouns for things.

sources.what: Monastic sign languages: earliest Benedictine sign books from about 1075 (and about 1083) at Cluny; signs used when silence was required (the nighttime Great Silence); mostly nouns for foods, clothing, rooms and buildings, ritual objects; few verbs such as sit, stand up, kneel, confess

items.notes: History (medieval religious life). Detail from one sentence, paraphrased (objects and places of monastic life). Attributed to historians, not to Scott G. Bruce by name (the source lists his book but not its content).

items.passage: In 1887, astronomers meeting in Paris launched a plan to photograph the whole sky and record the positions of millions of stars. Twenty observatories took part, each responsible for one band of the sky, and the stars on each of their glass plates had to be measured by eye and recorded by hand. In the early twentieth century, Johann Hagen, director of the Vatican Observatory, recruited four nuns from the Sisters of the Holy Child Mary, among them Emilia Ponzoni and Regina Colombo, to do this work. The sisters helped catalog nearly half a million stars.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about the sisters recruited by Hagen?
options: They measured every star photographed by the twenty observatories in the project.
They photographed the observatory’s band of the sky, leaving the measuring of the plates to astronomers.
They began measuring stars at the observatory several years before the project was launched in 1887.
They helped measure and record by hand the positions of hundreds of thousands of stars.
items.explanation: The text says the stars on each plate had to be measured by eye and recorded by hand, that Hagen recruited the sisters to do this work, and that they helped catalog nearly half a million stars. Choice D restates this.

A.why_wrong: The sky was divided among twenty observatories, each responsible for one band, and the text credits the sisters with helping catalog nearly half a million stars, not every star in the project.

B.why_wrong: Hagen recruited the sisters to measure and record the stars on the plates, the work described in the sentence before; the text never says they took the photographs.

C.why_wrong: The project was launched in 1887, and Hagen recruited the sisters in the early twentieth century.

sources.what: Vatican Observatory: Father John (Johann Georg) Hagen, director 1906 to 1930, recruited nuns from the Sisters of the Holy Child Mary (Emilia Ponzoni, Regina Colombo, Concetta Finardi, Luigia Panceri) for the recording and calculations of the Carte du Ciel; they helped map and catalog nearly half a million stars
Carte du Ciel: launched in 1887 at the Paris Astrographic Congress; 20 observatories, each with a declination zone; positions of millions of stars; plates measured by eye and recorded by hand

items.notes: History of science (astronomy). Written in review to replace the Ghost Army draft (topic fame: inflatable tanks, sound trucks, Ellsworth Kelly and the 1996 declassification are the whole popular profile, PBS 2013, Congressional Gold Medal 2022). Explicit detail across two sentences (this work points back to measuring by eye and recording by hand); key paraphrased (hundreds of thousands for nearly half a million). Claimed in claims.txt.

fixes: subject replaced: the draft was accurate, but inflatable tanks, sound trucks, Ellsworth Kelly and the 1996 declassification are the whole popular Ghost Army profile (PBS 2013, Congressional Gold Medal 2022), a topic-fame tell even without the nickname; new subject the Vatican Observatory sisters who measured Carte du Ciel plates (claimed in claims.txt), same template, tier, key letter D and recipes (overstated, twisted, contradicts); sources Vatican Observatory and Carte du Ciel; re-solved blind, D only

items.passage:
The following text is from Hermann Sudermann’s 1887 novel Dame Care (translated by Bertha Overbeck). Paul is a young man who runs his family’s farm. Michel Raudszus is one of the farm’s workers.

[Michel] was a silent, surly fellow, who did his work faultlessly and went off without grumbling when he was not wanted any more, but appeared again punctually as soon as there was fresh work. Paul did not like him at first, he was so laconic and reserved, and his sullen behavior had made an uncomfortable impression upon him; but then it suddenly occurred to him that he behaved in much the same way himself, and from that hour he had begun to like him heartily.
items.stem: According to the text, why does Paul come to like Michel?
options: Paul realizes that Michel’s quiet, guarded manner is much like his own.
Michel always returns on time whenever there is new work to be done.
Michel stops acting sullen once he and Paul get to know each other.
Paul learns that Michel complains only when he is not needed on the farm.
items.explanation: The text says Paul disliked Michel at first for being laconic and reserved, but then it occurred to Paul that he behaved in much the same way himself, and from then on he liked Michel. Choice A states this reason.

B.why_wrong: Michel does reappear punctually when there is work, but the text gives Paul’s recognition of himself in Michel as the reason for the change.

C.why_wrong: The text never says Michel’s behavior changed; it is Paul’s view of that behavior that changes.

D.why_wrong: The text says Michel went off without grumbling when he was not wanted.

sources.what: Sudermann, Dame Care, translated by Bertha Overbeck (Project Gutenberg), chapter IX, paragraph beginning He was a silent, surly fellow; Frau Sorge first published 1887

items.notes: Literature (German novel in translation). Excerpt copied exactly from the Gutenberg text; only change is [Michel] for He (the name is given in the preceding paragraph). Translation year omitted (not printed in the Gutenberg file).

review.note: excerpt checked against the Project Gutenberg text: exact (only [Michel] for He)

items.passage: Most vertebrates cannot survive for long without oxygen: when their cells are forced to generate energy without it, a by-product called lactate accumulates to damaging levels. The crucian carp, a fish inhabiting ponds and lakes in northern Europe, is a remarkable exception. In winter, ice can seal its ponds off from the atmosphere, and the water may become completely depleted of oxygen. Biologists have determined that the fish converts lactate into ethanol, which it excretes into the surrounding water rather than accumulating in its tissues, and in experiments crucian carp have survived without oxygen for 140 days.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The crucian carp avoids oxygen-poor water in winter by moving from frozen ponds into larger lakes.
Biologists have found that ethanol stored in the crucian carp’s tissues helps protect it from freezing temperatures.
The crucian carp can survive long periods without oxygen because it turns a harmful by-product into a substance it can release.
Unlike most vertebrates, the crucian carp produces energy without forming lactate when the water around it runs out of oxygen.
items.explanation: The text explains that lactate builds up to harmful levels in most vertebrates without oxygen, but that the crucian carp converts lactate into ethanol and releases it into the water, surviving without oxygen for 140 days in experiments. Choice C states this finding in general terms.

A.why_wrong: The text says the fish survives in ponds sealed by ice; it never says it moves elsewhere.

B.why_wrong: The fish releases ethanol into the water rather than storing it, and the text does not link ethanol to resisting cold.

D.why_wrong: The carp does form lactate; what sets it apart is that it converts the lactate into ethanol.

sources.what: Crucian carp: survives long periods in oxygen-depleted water by fermentation; ice seals ponds from atmospheric oxygen; pyruvate made from lactate and turned into acetaldehyde and ethanol, which is excreted into the water rather than accumulating; experimental fish kept anoxic for 140 days

items.notes: Natural science (physiology). Explainer passage, finding in the last sentence; key abstracts lactate and ethanol into a harmful by-product and a substance it can release. Key is the longest option here on purpose (batch key-longest rate).

review.note: topic fame borderline: goldfish and crucian carp making alcohol was a 2017 news item, but the passage frames it as physiology, not a headline; kept

items.passage: Between 1907 and 1918, ethnographer Gilbert Wilson interviewed Waheenee, also known as Buffalo Bird Woman, a Hidatsa woman living on the Fort Berthold Reservation in North Dakota; her son, Edward Goodbird, served as interpreter. Waheenee had farmed in the traditional Hidatsa way all her life, and she explained in detail how Hidatsa women planted and tended corn, squash, beans, and sunflowers, how they stored food for winter, and how they made their garden tools. In 1917 Wilson published her account, which he left largely unchanged, as Agriculture of the Hidatsa Indians: An Indian Interpretation.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Wilson learned to speak Hidatsa so that he could record Waheenee’s account of her people’s farming without an interpreter.
Wilson’s interviews with Waheenee produced a detailed record, largely in her own words, of how Hidatsa women farmed.
After reading Wilson’s book, many Hidatsa families returned to the farming methods that Waheenee had described.
Waheenee taught her son, Edward Goodbird, the Hidatsa farming methods that he later described to Wilson.
items.explanation: The text says Wilson interviewed Waheenee over about a decade, that she explained in detail how Hidatsa women grew, stored, and worked their crops, and that he published her account largely unchanged. Choice B states this main point.

A.why_wrong: The text says Waheenee’s son, Edward Goodbird, served as interpreter, so Wilson did not work without one.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how Hidatsa families responded to Wilson’s book.

D.why_wrong: Waheenee herself explained the farming methods; Goodbird served as interpreter.

sources.what: Buffalo Bird Woman (Waheenee, about 1839 to 1932): Gilbert Wilson interviewed her 1907 to 1918 with her son Edward Goodbird interpreting; she gardened in the traditional Hidatsa way all her life; her account of Hidatsa agriculture (sunflowers, corn, squashes, beans, storing for winter, tools) was published in 1917 as Agriculture of the Hidatsa Indians: An Indian Interpretation, left essentially unchanged by Wilson

items.notes: History (Native American agriculture, ethnography). Written in review to replace the Project Pigeon draft (topic fame: Skinner’s pigeon-guided bomb is intro-psychology textbook trivia, with a 2024 Ig Nobel). Main idea spread over the passage; key paraphrases left largely unchanged as largely in her own words. Claimed in claims.txt.

fixes: subject replaced: Skinner’s pigeon-guided bomb is intro-psychology textbook trivia (2024 Ig Nobel), a topic-fame tell even without the name Project Pigeon; new subject Gilbert Wilson’s 1907 to 1918 interviews with Waheenee (Buffalo Bird Woman) on Hidatsa farming (claimed in claims.txt), same template, tier, key letter B and recipe types; source Wikipedia Buffalo Bird Woman; re-solved blind, B only

items.passage: After Mozambique’s long civil war ended in 1992, a program run by the Christian Council of Mozambique collected weapons from the population and had them deactivated. Artist Gonçalo Mabunda, born in Maputo in 1975, transforms these decommissioned weapons into sculpture. He welds rifles, pistols, rocket launchers, and shell casings into anthropomorphic figures, into masks inspired by traditional African designs, and into elaborate thrones, works that challenge the assumption that political authority must rest on force.
items.stem: Which choice best states the text’s main idea about Mabunda?
options: He collected weapons from Mozambicans through a project that he founded after the civil war.
He began making sculptures from weapons in 1975, while the civil war was still being fought.
He is best known for his masks, which museums display alongside traditional African masks.
He turns weapons of war into art that draws on tradition and comments on power.
items.explanation: The text says Mabunda makes figures, masks drawing on traditional African designs, and thrones out of deactivated weapons from Mozambique’s civil war, works that question the idea that power rests on force. Choice D generalizes these examples.

A.why_wrong: The text says the weapons were collected by a project run by the Christian Council of Mozambique, not one Mabunda founded.

B.why_wrong: Mabunda was born in 1975; the text says the weapons were collected after the war ended in 1992.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions his masks but never says they are his best-known works or describes how museums display them.

sources.what: Gonçalo Mabunda (born 1975, Maputo): works with deactivated weapons from the Mozambican Civil War (Kalashnikovs, rockets, pistols, shell casings) collected by a Christian Council of Mozambique project; makes anthropomorphic figures, thrones and masks drawing on traditional designs; thrones challenge the idea that power rests on weapons

items.notes: Arts (sculpture). Profile; key generalizes the three kinds of works. The war’s end in 1992 (Rome General Peace Accords) is common knowledge; the program’s name is left out (sources disagree on it).

items.passage:
The following text is from Emily Lawless’s 1892 novel Grania: The Story of an Island. Grania lives on Inishmaan, one of the Aran Islands off the west coast of Ireland. Murdough is a young man from the island whom she has known since childhood.

Grania was hardly listening. She wanted—she hardly herself knew what she wanted—but certainly it was not words. Why would Murdough always go on talk, talk, talking? she thought irritably. She admired his interminable flow of words of course—she would not have been Irish had she not done so—at the same time she was conscious of a vague grudge against them. They seemed always to be coming between them. They were her rivals after a fashion, and she was not of a temper to put up patiently with rivals, even invisible ones.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Grania admires Murdough’s way with words but resents it because she feels it keeps the two of them apart.
Grania is jealous of other young women on the island who admire the way Murdough speaks.
Grania wishes that she could speak as easily and impressively as Murdough does.
Grania has stopped listening to Murdough because she no longer admires the things he says.
items.explanation: Grania admires Murdough’s endless flow of words but holds a grudge against them because they seem always to come between the two of them, like rivals. Choice A captures both her admiration and her resentment.

B.why_wrong: The rivals Grania resents are Murdough’s words themselves, “even invisible ones,” not other young women.

C.why_wrong: The text says Grania wants something other than words; it never says she wishes to speak as he does.

D.why_wrong: Grania is hardly listening, but the text says she admires his flow of words.

sources.what: Emily Lawless, Grania: The Story of an Island (1892), Project Gutenberg text, paragraph beginning Grania was hardly listening; Murdough is her childhood playfellow and neighbor on Inishmaan

items.notes: Literature (Irish novel). Excerpt copied exactly; house style only: double hyphens to closed em dashes, the italic what set roman.

review.note: excerpt checked against the Project Gutenberg text: exact (double hyphens set as closed em dashes, italic what set roman)

items.passage: Jumping spiders of the genus Portia, found in parts of Africa, Asia, and Australia, frequently prey on other spiders by invading their webs. A Portia plucks and vibrates the silk, generating signals that can resemble those of an entangled insect or of a male spider courting a female. It does not simply repeat one fixed signal, however: researchers including Robert Jackson have found that Portia experiments with different patterns of vibration and, when one of them lures the web’s resident closer, continues using that pattern.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can most likely be concluded about Portia jumping spiders?
options: They likely catch more insects than spiders because insects respond more readily to their signals.
They likely adjust their hunting behavior to suit the particular spider they are trying to catch.
They likely produce a single kind of vibration that every web-building spider mistakes for prey.
They likely learned their signals by watching male spiders court females in nearby webs.
items.explanation: The text says Portia tries different vibrations and keeps using whichever one draws the web’s owner closer. It follows that the spider adjusts its signals to the response of the particular spider it is hunting.

A.why_wrong: The text says Portia often hunts other spiders and never compares how many insects and spiders it catches.

C.why_wrong: The text says Portia does not repeat one fixed signal but tries different patterns.

D.why_wrong: Some signals resemble courtship, but the text never says how Portia acquired them.

sources.what: Portia (spider): aggressive mimicry by vibrating webs to imitate trapped insects or courting males; instinctive tactics are starting points for trial and error, adjusting signals until the prey responds; research by Robert R. Jackson, Fiona R. Cross and others

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). One-step inference from the trial-and-error sentence. Portia is not in the bank, claims or official items.

items.passage: Roman gladiators are often imagined as hulking fighters who consumed enormous quantities of meat, but ancient writers sometimes referred to them as “barley eaters.” A chemical analysis of skeletons from a gladiator cemetery at Ephesus, in present-day Turkey, supports the ancient designation. Sandra Lösch and colleagues determined that the gladiators, like other inhabitants of the city, ate mainly plant foods such as wheat and barley. Their bones did differ in one respect: the ratio of strontium to calcium was nearly twice as high, which the researchers suggest might reflect a beverage made from plant ash.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Gladiators at Ephesus ate more meat than other residents did, which explains the unusual chemistry of their bones.
The chemical study indicates that ancient writers exaggerated how much barley gladiators ate.
Bones from Ephesus suggest that gladiators ate largely the same plant-based diet as other residents, with one possible addition.
Gladiators at Ephesus were given a plant-ash beverage in place of the barley that other residents ate.
items.explanation: The text sets the common image of meat-eating gladiators against a bone study at Ephesus showing that gladiators, like other residents, ate mainly wheat and barley, with a higher strontium-to-calcium ratio that might reflect a plant-ash beverage. Choice C states the finding and keeps the hedge.

A.why_wrong: The study found the gladiators ate mainly plant foods, like other residents; the higher ratio is linked to a possible plant-ash beverage, not meat.

B.why_wrong: The text says the study supports the ancient label of “barley eaters.”

D.why_wrong: The gladiators, like other residents, ate mainly wheat and barley; the possible plant-ash beverage is offered only as an explanation for one difference in their bones.

sources.what: Lösch et al. 2014 (PLOS ONE), 22 gladiators from Ephesus: all individuals ate C3 plants like wheat and barley as staples, no significant isotope difference between gladiators and non-gladiators; Sr/Ca almost twice as high in gladiators, which might suggest a plant-ash beverage

items.notes: Archaeology. View then correction (popular image vs bone chemistry). Barley eaters (hordearii) is the derogatory nickname the paper cites from ancient sources; Pliny’s ash beverage was served after fights, so no distractor names a purpose for it. Key keeps the might (one possible addition).

items.passage: Rebetiko, a genre of urban song typically accompanied by the bouzouki, flourished in Greek port cities during the 1920s and 1930s. Its origins lay elsewhere, however: early in the twentieth century, the music’s principal center was Smyrna, a cosmopolitan Anatolian port with a large Greek community. How did a music centered in Smyrna come to thrive in Greek cities? Much of the answer lies in the population exchange of 1923, which brought enormous numbers of refugees from Anatolia to Greek harbors such as Piraeus. Among them were accomplished musicians, some of whom later directed recording sessions for major record companies.
items.stem: Which question does the text most directly attempt to answer?
options: Which instruments were most commonly played on early rebetiko recordings?
When were the first rebetiko songs recorded in Smyrna?
Why did many Greek musicians leave Piraeus for Anatolia after 1923?
What led a style of music associated with Smyrna to flourish in Greek cities?
items.explanation: The text asks how a music centered in Smyrna came to thrive in Greek cities and answers that the 1923 population exchange brought many refugees, including skilled musicians, to Greek ports. Choice D restates that question.

A.recipe: on-topic question the text never takes up
A.why_wrong: The text mentions the bouzouki but never discusses which instruments were most common on recordings.

B.recipe: on-topic question the text never takes up
B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about when rebetiko was first recorded in Smyrna.

C.why_wrong: The text describes refugees, including musicians, moving from Anatolia to Greek ports, not musicians leaving Piraeus.

sources.what: Rebetiko: main center in the early 20th century was Smyrna; after the 1923 population exchange huge numbers of refugees settled in Piraeus and other ports; many were skilled musicians, some became studio directors for major record companies (Peristeris, Toundas)

items.notes: Arts and history (music). Question-then-answer passage; the key paraphrases the passage’s own question.

items.passage: For decades, until the 1920s, a group of killer whales cooperated with whalers at Twofold Bay, near the town of Eden in southeastern Australia. The killer whales herded large baleen whales into the bay and alerted the whalers by splashing near their station. After the whalers had harpooned a whale, they anchored the carcass in the water so that the killer whales could consume its tongue and lips. The whalers retained the remainder of the animal, including its valuable blubber and bones.
items.stem: According to the text, what did the killer whales get from working with the whalers?
options: Certain parts of each whale that was caught
Protection from other whalers who hunted killer whales
Food that the whalers brought from the town of Eden
The blubber and bones of the whales that were caught
items.explanation: The text says the whalers anchored each harpooned whale’s carcass in the water so the killer whales could consume its tongue and lips. Choice A states this.

B.why_wrong: The text never mentions other whalers or any protection for the killer whales.

C.why_wrong: Eden is named only as the nearby town; the killer whales fed on parts of the whales that had been caught.

D.why_wrong: The text says the whalers retained the rest of each whale, including its blubber and bones.

sources.what: Old Tom and the killers of Eden, Twofold Bay: the orca pod herded baleen whales into the bay, Old Tom flop-tailed near the Davidson whaling station to alert the whalers, the carcass was anchored so the orcas could eat the tongue and lips (the law of the tongue), the whalers kept blubber and bones; ended in the 1920s

items.notes: Natural science and history. Noun-phrase options without final periods, as in the official 1.4 and 1.9.

review.note: topic fame borderline: the killers of Eden are an Australian museum story, not textbook; kept

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Fredrika Bremer’s 1839 novel The Home (translated by Mary Howitt). Petrea, a young girl, got lost during a family outing and fell into a thicket of bushes before she was found.

After Petrea’s scratches and bruises had been washed, the mother permitted the children to have a supper of pancakes and raspberry-cream, in order to console them for the unfortunate expedition. Hereupon the children danced for joy about the table; and Petrea, who, on account of her misfortunes, received [the largest share], regarded it as certain that they always eat such cream in heaven, wherefore she proposed that it should be called “Angels’ food.”
items.stem: According to the text, why does the mother let the children have pancakes and raspberry cream for supper?
options: She wants to celebrate the creation of a new family dish.
She wants to comfort them after their outing went badly.
She wants to reward them for the raspberries they picked.
She wants to thank them for helping to find Petrea.
items.explanation: The text says the mother allowed the supper “in order to console them for the unfortunate expedition.” Choice B restates this reason.

A.why_wrong: Petrea names the dish “Angels’ food” only after the supper is served; the new name is a result of the supper, not its purpose.

C.why_wrong: The text calls the expedition unfortunate and never mentions the children picking raspberries.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the children helping to find Petrea.

sources.what: Fredrika Bremer, The Home; or, Life in Sweden, translated by Mary Howitt (Project Gutenberg), the paragraph beginning After Petrea’s scratches and bruises; Hemmet first published 1839

items.notes: Literature (Swedish novel in translation). Adapted: with Riga-balsam cut after washed; a Benjamin’s portion glossed as [the largest share]; text stops at Angels’ food. Translation year omitted (not printed in the Gutenberg file).

review.note: excerpt checked against the Project Gutenberg text: exact apart from the marked adaptation (with Riga-balsam cut, a Benjamin’s portion glossed)

items.passage: The hamerkop, a brown wading bird found mainly in Africa, constructs one of the largest nests of any bird: a domed structure of sticks and mud that can measure more than 1.5 meters across and is sturdy enough to support a person’s weight. A pair of hamerkops builds three to five of these nests annually, regardless of whether the birds are breeding. Many of the nests eventually shelter other animals. Owls sometimes evict the hamerkops and occupy a nest, and snakes and small mammals may settle in abandoned ones.
items.stem: According to the text, what is true about hamerkop nests?
options: Each one is used by the same pair of hamerkops for many years.
Hamerkops build them only in years when the birds are breeding.
They often become homes for other kinds of animals.
They are built by owls and later taken over by hamerkops.
items.explanation: The text says many hamerkop nests eventually shelter other animals, such as owls, snakes, and small mammals. Choice C states this.

A.why_wrong: A pair builds three to five nests annually, and owls sometimes take nests over.

B.why_wrong: The text says hamerkops build nests regardless of whether they are breeding.

D.why_wrong: Hamerkops build the nests; owls sometimes evict them and occupy the nests.

sources.what: Hamerkop: nest sometimes more than 1.5 m across and strong enough to support a man’s weight; three to five nests a year whether breeding or not; barn owls and eagle owls may force hamerkops out; owls, snakes, genets and other small mammals use abandoned nests

items.notes: Natural science (birds). One-sentence detail, key paraphrased (housing other animals as homes for other kinds of animals).

items.passage: The Morning Glory is an unusual cloud formation consisting of long rolls, sometimes stretching up to 1,000 kilometers, that travel low across the sky. The southern Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Australia is the only location where it can be predicted and observed regularly, typically between late September and early November, and the town of Burketown attracts glider pilots who hope to ride alongside it. Researchers have proposed several explanations for the phenomenon. One, offered in 1981, connects it to sea breezes that converge over the nearby Cape York Peninsula.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Glider pilots first described the Morning Glory cloud in 1981 after flying near Burketown.
The Morning Glory cloud forms only over Cape York Peninsula, where sea breezes meet.
Morning Glory clouds are common across Australia but are largest over the Gulf of Carpentaria.
A rare cloud forms predictably in one part of Australia, and researchers have tried to explain how it forms.
items.explanation: The text describes the Morning Glory cloud, says the southern Gulf of Carpentaria is the only place where it can be predicted and observed regularly, and notes that researchers have proposed explanations for it. Choice D sums up these points.

A.why_wrong: 1981 is when one explanation was offered; the text never says glider pilots first described the cloud.

B.why_wrong: The cloud is observed over the southern Gulf of Carpentaria; Cape York Peninsula is where one explanation says the sea breezes meet.

C.why_wrong: The text says the cloud is unusual and can be predicted and observed regularly only over the southern Gulf of Carpentaria.

sources.what: Morning Glory cloud: southern Gulf of Carpentaria the only known place where it can be predicted and observed regularly; late September to early November; up to 1,000 km long; Burketown attracts glider pilots; R. H. Clarke’s 1981 hypothesis of sea breezes meeting over Cape York Peninsula, later studies propose other models

items.notes: Earth science (meteorology). Explainer; main idea spread over the passage. The 1981 author (R. H. Clarke) is left unnamed. Key is the longest option here on purpose (batch key-longest rate).

review.note: topic fame borderline: the Morning Glory cloud is a weather-curiosity staple; kept as an easy explainer, but it is the batch’s most familiar subject

items.passage: Centuries ago, a mudslide buried part of a Makah village at Ozette, on the Pacific shore of present-day Washington State. The mud sealed several houses and everything inside them. After storm waves exposed some of the buried objects in 1970, members of the Makah Tribe and archaeologists spent eleven years carefully excavating the site. They recovered more than 55,000 artifacts, roughly 30,000 of them made of wood, a material that ordinarily decomposes. Many of these objects are now exhibited at the Makah Cultural and Research Center.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Archaeologists have learned that the Makah left Ozette after a storm damaged the village in 1970.
A mudslide preserved normally perishable objects, allowing many Makah artifacts to be recovered.
Most of the artifacts found at Ozette were made of stone, since objects made of wood rarely survive.
The Makah Cultural and Research Center was built at Ozette to protect the village from future mudslides.
items.explanation: The text says a mudslide sealed houses and their contents at Ozette, and that after a storm exposed them, the Makah and archaeologists recovered more than 55,000 artifacts, many of wood, which ordinarily decomposes. Choice B states this main point.

A.why_wrong: The 1970 storm exposed buried objects; the village had been buried by a mudslide centuries earlier.

C.why_wrong: About 30,000 of the more than 55,000 artifacts were made of wood.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that many objects are displayed at the center; it says nothing about its location or purpose.

sources.what: Ozette Indian Village Archeological Site: a mudslide engulfed part of a Makah village (radiocarbon about 1560, elsewhere about 1750); a storm in February 1970 exposed well-preserved wooden artifacts; excavation lasted 11 years with Makah and Washington State University archaeologists; more than 55,000 artifacts, about 30,000 wooden; many shown at the Makah Cultural and Research Center

items.notes: Archaeology. Mudslide date given as centuries ago (the source gives two dates); no excavation leader named.

items.passage:
The following text is from Peter Rosegger’s 1875 novel The Forest Schoolmaster (translated by Frances E. Skinner in 1901). After years of travel and war, the narrator has come to live in a remote mountain forest.

I already feel contented in the woods. The few people who see me going about in the forest gaze after me, unable to understand why I, a young fellow, should be roaming here in the wilderness. Ah yes, it is true, from day to day I am growing younger and am beginning to take a new lease of life. I am recovering. That comes from the fresh, primitive nature which surrounds me.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The narrator feels renewed by life in the forest, even though others cannot understand why he is there.
The narrator is lonely in the forest and wishes that more people would come to visit him.
The narrator is slowly recovering from a serious illness with the help of plants that he gathers in the forest.
The narrator is puzzled by the local people who spend their days roaming in the wilderness.
items.explanation: The narrator says he feels contented in the woods, that he is growing younger and recovering because of the nature around him, and that the few people who see him cannot understand why he is there. Choice A captures his feeling and the others’ puzzlement.

B.why_wrong: The narrator says he feels contented; he never says he is lonely or wants visitors.

C.why_wrong: His recovery comes from the fresh, primitive nature around him; the text mentions no illness or plants used as remedies.

D.why_wrong: It is the local people who cannot understand why the narrator roams the wilderness.

sources.what: Peter Rosegger, The Forest Schoolmaster, translated by Frances E. Skinner (Putnam, 1901), Project Gutenberg text, section Peace of the Primeval Forest; Die Schriften des Waldschulmeisters first published 1875

items.notes: Literature (Austrian novel in translation, a schoolmaster’s journal). Excerpt copied exactly. The narrator, Andreas Erdmann, has come to the Winkel after war and wandering (preceding paragraphs).

review.note: excerpt checked against the Project Gutenberg text: exact; translator and 1901 Putnam edition confirmed

items.passage: In 1967, civil rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer founded the Freedom Farm Cooperative in Sunflower County, Mississippi, to help impoverished Black families feed themselves and become more economically independent. The cooperative initially owned 40 acres of farmland and eventually expanded to 600. One of its programs was a “pig bank”: participating families borrowed a pig, raised it, and could use it for food after it had produced piglets. Beginning with a donation of 55 pigs, the bank had accumulated about 2,000 pigs within three years.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Hamer started the cooperative to raise money for civil rights campaigns in other states.
The cooperative bought 2,000 pigs from local farmers during its first three years.
Hamer’s cooperative used land and animals to help families produce their own food and become more independent.
Families who joined the cooperative were required to give up farming their own land.
items.explanation: The text says Hamer founded the cooperative to help impoverished Black families feed themselves and become more economically independent, and describes its land and its pig bank. Choice C generalizes these examples.

A.why_wrong: The text gives the cooperative’s purpose as helping families feed themselves; it never mentions raising money for other campaigns.

B.why_wrong: The pig bank began with a donation of 55 pigs and grew to about 2,000; the text never says pigs were bought.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about families giving up their own land.

sources.what: Freedom Farm Cooperative: founded 1967 by Fannie Lou Hamer in Sunflower County, Mississippi; began with 40 acres, 600 by 1972; pig bank began with 55 pigs donated by the National Council of Negro Women and reached about 2,000 in three years; pigs loaned to families, harvested after producing piglets; goals of nutrition and self-sufficiency

items.notes: History (civil rights, agriculture). Profile; key generalizes land and pig bank. Key is the longest option here on purpose (batch key-longest rate).
